observation.visible_scene: A night polar landscape: a star-filled sky with the Milky Way band on the left, a green aurora (northern lights) glowing above a ridge of dark, jagged mountains, and a calm, glassy water/ice surface in the foreground that mirrors the aurora. The mountains, stars, and Milky Way hold fixed screen positions throughout.
visible_changes: The bright green aurora column/curtain drifts slowly leftward over the excerpt: its luminous core moves from roughly center (early frames) toward the left third (late frames), while its shape stretches and reshapes in place.
The lower horizon glow of the aurora, initially near center behind the peak, also shifts left and dims slightly.
A faint secondary green patch becomes visible on the right side of the sky in the later frames that was absent at the start.
The foreground reflection tracks the sky aurora: the bright green mirror patch in the water moves left and breaks into smaller, dimmer fragments as the source light shifts.
The terrain, mountain silhouettes, and starfield show no positional change, indicating the visible motion belongs to the aurora and its reflection rather than to the camera or landscape.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the leftward aurora drift continues, reverses, or completes a cycle beyond this segment is unknown.
The physical cause or intensity evolution of the aurora is not shown.
Any camera motion outside these frames is unknown.
uncertain_details: The exact speed and whether the aurora's apparent leftward movement is pure translation versus deformation-in-place is hard to separate.
A very slight camera drift cannot be fully ruled out, though the fixed star/mountain positions argue against significant camera movement.
The water surface is treated as a reflective plane; its ripples/texture changes are subtle and not clearly separable from the moving reflection.
